# Project layout {#sec-layout}

A good layout shows where things are before anyone reads a line of code. C++ has no
official standard for it, but it has a widely used convention, and Qt Quick adds a few rules
of its own.

## A conventional top level {#sec-pitchfork}

Base your layout on **Pitchfork**, the most widely used convention for C++ project layouts.
It is a guideline, not a standard: no tool enforces it, and projects adapt it to their needs.
An application could look like this:

```{.default filename="my-app/"}
my-app/
├── CMakeLists.txt
├── CMakePresets.json
├── cmake/        build helpers
├── docs/         documentation
├── external/     third-party code kept in the repository
├── libs/         libraries that could live without the app
├── src/          the application
└── tests/        tests for src/
```

Pitchfork itself allows either a single `src/` or a split into `libs/`, but never both. An
application with separable libraries often uses both anyway, as above: the app goes in
`src/`, and anything that could live without it goes in `libs/`. Other names are common too:
Qt and many older projects name this folder `3rdparty/` instead of `external/`, and Google's
projects use `third_party/`. Which names you pick
matters less than using them consistently, so that code is where a reader expects it.

::: {.more}
**Template:** the repository root

**Read more:** [Pitchfork](https://joholl.github.io/pitchfork-website/)
:::

## Public and private headers {#sec-include-dirs}

A library's headers fall into two groups. **Public headers** are its API: other code includes
them, and they ship when you install the library. **Private headers** hold implementation
details that only the library's own sources include. Keep the two apart, so that nobody can
depend on a detail by accident.

The most common way is to give the public headers a folder of their own, `include/<name>/`:

```{.default filename="libs/core/"}
core/
├── CMakeLists.txt
├── include/
│   └── core/
│       └── message.h        public: consumers include it
└── src/
    ├── message.cpp
    ├── peerregistry.hpp     private: invisible to consumers
    └── peerregistry.cpp
```

```{.cmake filename="libs/core/CMakeLists.txt"}
add_library(core STATIC src/message.cpp src/peerregistry.cpp)
target_include_directories(core
    PUBLIC include   # <1>
    PRIVATE src      # <2>
)
```
1. Consumers get `include/` on their include path and write `#include <core/message.h>`.
2. Only the library itself can include `peerregistry.hpp`.

The extra `core/` folder pays off at every include. `#include <core/message.h>` says where
the header comes from and cannot collide with another library's `message.h`. The suffix can
mark the split as well: this guide uses `.h` for public headers, which ship, and `.hpp` for
everything else. Many projects use one suffix for both, which works just as well.

It is not the only way. Qt keeps all of its headers next to the sources, and its build
generates the public include folder (`include/QtCore/`) from them. Private headers end in
`_p.h`, install into a separate folder, and carry no compatibility promise. The mechanism
differs; the separation is the same.

Code that never leaves the application can keep things simpler. The feature folders under `src/`
(@sec-features) keep all their headers next to the sources and put that folder on their
include path. Whatever links `app_canvas` can write `#include "CanvasStore.hpp"`; whatever
does not, cannot. The build still enforces the boundary (@sec-direction); there is no
separate public API.

::: {.more}
**Template:** `libs/shapes/`, which declares its public headers as a `FILE_SET HEADERS`, the
modern spelling of `PUBLIC include`; `src/canvas/` for a feature folder
:::

## Namespaces keep the global scope empty {#sec-namespaces}

A name declared outside any namespace can collide with the same name in every other library
of the program: two `Point` types, two `distance()` functions. At best the compiler stops
with an error. At worst the linker quietly keeps one of two different definitions, and the
program misbehaves at run time. Put all of your code into a namespace, named like the
library and its include folder:

```{.cpp filename="include/shapes/Recognizer.h"}
namespace shapes {

struct Point { double x = 0.0; double y = 0.0; };

class Recognizer { /* ... */ };

} // namespace shapes
```

```{.cpp filename="src/Recognizer.cpp"}
namespace shapes {
namespace {

double distance(Point a, Point b);   // only this file sees it

} // namespace
} // namespace shapes
```

Three more rules keep names from leaking:

- **File-local helpers go into an unnamed namespace.** Other files cannot see them, and two
  files can each have their own `distance()`.
- **No `using namespace` at file scope in a header.** It would apply to every file that
  includes the header, now and later. Inside a `.cpp` file or a function it is fine.
- **Macros ignore namespaces.** Give each one a prefix unique to your project, such as
  `SHAPES_`, or use a `constexpr` variable or an inline function instead.

For a library this is part of its API: a consumer cannot rename what your headers leak. An
application shares its process with Qt and every other dependency, so the same rules apply
to it, nested by feature: `app::canvas`, `app::sketchbook`.

You can see two eras in Qt itself. Its classes start with `Q` because Qt is older than reliable
namespace support in compilers; its newer APIs live in namespaces such as `Qt::` and
`QtConcurrent::`. Classes with `Q_OBJECT` or `QML_ELEMENT` work inside namespaces, and QML
sees the class name without the namespace. One catch: in `Q_PROPERTY`, signals and
`Q_INVOKABLE` methods, write other types fully qualified (`app::canvas::CanvasStore *`).
moc and the QML tools read those as text and do not resolve names from the enclosing
namespace.

::: {.callout-important}
## A public header is a promise
Everything in a public header becomes API: consumers include it, build against it, and break
when it changes. Keep it to what they need, inside your namespace, with no `using namespace`
and no unprefixed macros. Code that only your own sources share belongs in a private
header, where you can change it freely. Before a header moves into `include/`, ask whether a
consumer really has to see it.
:::

::: {.more}
**Template:** `libs/shapes/include/shapes/Recognizer.h`, `src/canvas/Sketch.hpp`

**Read more:** [C++ Core Guidelines, SF.20 to SF.22](https://isocpp.github.io/CppCoreGuidelines/CppCoreGuidelines#rs-namespace)
:::

## Separable code becomes its own library {#sec-separable}

Ask of every piece of code: *would someone use this without our app?* An algorithm, a file
parser or a protocol passes that test. It then becomes a library under `libs/`, with its own
tests and, ideally, no Qt at all.

Such a library is the easiest code in the project to test, to reason about, and to reuse.
Code that only serves one feature fails the test and stays inside that feature.

::: {.more}
**Template:** `libs/shapes/`, a shape recognizer in plain C++. It does not link Qt, so a Qt
include there fails to compile.
:::

## Group by feature, then by role {#sec-features}

Organize the application by feature, not by file type. A feature folder holds everything
the feature needs: its C++ types and its QML files, side by side, built as one QML module.

```{.default filename="src/"}
src/
├── app/            main.cpp, the main window
├── style/          the look: controls, colors, icons
├── canvas/         a small feature: a few files
└── contacts/       a grown feature, split by role
    ├── components/    reusable QML pieces: a search field, a delegate
    ├── pages/         screens that combine components
    ├── models/        item models
    └── controllers/   view models and controllers
```

Adding a feature adds a folder; removing it deletes one. Split by role only once a feature
outgrows a single folder.

::: {.more}
**Template:** `src/`

**Read more:** [Qt 6 QML project architecture](https://www.learnqt.guide/qt6-qml-project-architecture)
:::

## Tests mirror the sources {#sec-tests-mirror}

`tests/canvas/` tests `src/canvas/`. When you look for a class's tests, you know where they
are. A library under `libs/` keeps its tests in its own `tests/` folder, so it can move to
another repository in one piece.

::: {.more}
**Template:** `tests/` and `libs/shapes/tests/`
:::

## Include by module {#sec-include-style}

Write Qt includes with their module, and your own libraries' includes with their folder:

```cpp
#include <QtCore/QObject>
#include <QtQuick/QQuickItem>
#include <core/message.h>
```

Every include then tells the reader which module or library a type comes from, in the same
form for Qt and for your own code.
